prompt: For any capability gap, the correct order to try solutions is…

options.text: Prompting → RAG → fine-tuning → (almost never) training from scratch, stopping at the first rung that solves it
Fine-tuning first, since it's most powerful
Training from scratch for full control
RAG for everything, always

explanation: Climb the ladder only as far as needed. Skipping to fine-tuning for a prompt- or retrieval-shaped problem is the field's most common expensive mistake.

prompt: Fine-tuning is the WRONG tool for adding factual knowledge because…

options.text: …it's unreliable at teaching facts, bakes in a snapshot that goes stale, and can't cite sources: knowledge problems are retrieval's job
…it is always more expensive than any alternative
…it permanently damages the base model
…facts cannot be represented in weights at all

explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behavior/format/style far more than it installs reliable, current, citable knowledge. Use RAG for facts.

prompt: Which is fine-tuning's genuine sweet spot?

options.text: Consistent format/style/tone at scale, and shrinking prompts so a smaller, cheaper model can do a narrow job
Keeping the model's knowledge up to date daily
Per-user access control
Citing sources in answers

explanation: Bake in behavior, drop the lengthy instructions, often down-tier the model. Knowledge, freshness, access control, and citations are jobs for retrieval and code.

prompt: What do parameter-efficient methods like LoRA change about fine-tuning?

options.text: They adjust a small set of added weights instead of all parameters, making fine-tuning cheap enough for modest hardware or a hosted API
They let a model learn without any data
They eliminate the need to evaluate the result
They retrain the model from scratch faster

explanation: LoRA-style methods make fine-tuning accessible, but the hidden costs (a new artifact to version, eval, monitor, and re-tune) remain.

prompt: A hospital must process patient data that legally cannot leave its premises, at steady high volume. The fitting approach is…

options.text: …a self-hosted open-weight model (quantized to fit hardware), keeping data in-network with cost bounded by fixed infrastructure
…a hosted frontier API with a good privacy policy
…emailing records to an enterprise API tier
…fine-tuning a hosted model on the records

explanation: Hard data residency + steady volume is the canonical self-hosting case: data never leaves by construction, and fixed hardware amortizes. Any option sending data out fails the residency requirement.

prompt: Quantization makes local models practical by…

options.text: …storing weights at lower numeric precision (e.g., 16-bit → 4-bit), cutting memory and speeding inference for usually-small quality loss
…removing layers from the network
…deleting rare vocabulary tokens
…training the model on less data

explanation: Lower-precision weights shrink the memory footprint: often the difference between needing a data-center GPU and running on a good laptop.

prompt: A question requires connecting information from two separate documents. The most direct technique is…

options.text: Multi-hop retrieval: retrieve, read, then retrieve again to gather and connect information across sources
Raising the temperature
One giant chunk covering everything
Fine-tuning the generator on the two documents

explanation: Cross-document synthesis exceeds single-shot retrieval; multi-hop (an agentic retrieval loop) gathers the pieces iteratively: validated on your eval set before you pay the latency.

prompt: The unifying rule for adopting ANY advanced technique (advanced retrieval, fine-tuning, new architectures) is…

options.text: …measure the need and the gain on your own eval set for your own task before adding the complexity
…adopt whatever tops public benchmarks
…avoid all new techniques
…wait until the provider defaults to it

explanation: Benchmarks measure someone else's task. Evaluate on your data; every technique is a latency/complexity/maintenance cost that your numbers must justify.

prompt: Which best characterizes the durable, non-expiring skills this course built?

options.text: The primitives (tokens, embeddings, attention, retrieval, tool loops, evals) and the judgment (workflow-before-agent, evals-before-optimization, human authority): stable across model releases
Memorizing current model names and prices
One specific provider's SDK
The exact SOTA technique of this month

explanation: Models are new implementations of stable primitives; the stances and engineering discipline outlast every version churn.

prompt: Which capstone better demonstrates AI engineering?

options.text: A modest invoice-triage workflow that is evaluated (40-case suite, honest numbers), secured (threat model), deployed with monitoring, and measured (before/after ROI)
An impressive multi-agent research demo with no evals, no deployment, and no cost analysis
Whichever uses the most agents
Whichever has the largest model

explanation: The course's thesis: the engineering around the model is the job. Complete-and-coherent beats ambitious-and-hollow: the demo-not-system trap is the thing to avoid.

prompt: Asked in your defense 'which component causes most errors?', the strongest answer is…

options.text: A specific, measured, stage-localized answer backed by your eval breakdown and traces (e.g., 'retrieval: recall@5 is 68%, 71% of failures trace there')
'The model is unpredictable, so it's hard to say'
'There are no errors in my system'
'Whatever the last user complained about'

explanation: Evidence-backed, stage-localized precision is the signature of the discipline. Vagueness, denial, and anecdote signal it's missing.

prompt: Which elements must a passing capstone demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: An eval suite with graders and honest numbers, including failures
Safety: threat model, least privilege, approval on consequential actions
Deployment with monitoring, a budget/SLOs, and a rollback runbook
The largest possible model and maximum autonomy, regardless of the task

explanation: Evaluation, safety, and operations must all be present and coherent. Model size and autonomy are means chosen to fit the task, never goals in themselves.

prompt: Distillation (training a small model on a large model's outputs) is attractive when…

options.text: …a narrow task needs the big model's quality at small-model cost/latency: the student learns the specific behavior without the teacher's breadth
…you want the small model to gain general intelligence
…you have no eval set
…never; distillation is obsolete

explanation: A teacher-labeled dataset for one job transfers that job. Validate the student on YOUR evals; expect the narrow win, not general parity.

prompt: Synthetic training data (generated by a model) carries which core caution?

options.text: It inherits the generator's blind spots and can't be the sole evidence of real-world performance: real, held-out data must anchor evaluation
It is illegal in most countries
It is always superior to human data
It cannot be stored in JSON

explanation: Synthetic data expands coverage cheaply but circularly. The test set that decides anything must come from reality.

prompt: For fine-tuning, you split train/validation/test by distinct entities or time periods (not random rows) because…

options.text: …near-duplicate rows from the same entity landing in both train and test inflate scores: the leakage lessons of Module 5 apply fully to adaptation data
…random splits are computationally expensive
…entities have legal rights to one split
…it doesn't matter for fine-tuning

explanation: Same customer's ten similar invoices across splits = memorization measured as skill. Split on the axis of real-world generalization.

prompt: Quantization's accuracy cost shows up MOST in…

options.text: …tasks sensitive to small numerical distinctions and less-represented languages, which is why you re-run YOUR evals on the quantized model, not trust generic benchmarks
…file download speed
…the model's vocabulary size
…nothing; quantization is lossless

explanation: Precision loss is uneven across capabilities. The decision instrument is your task's eval before/after: the module's recurring answer.

prompt: Self-hosting adds which operational jobs that hosted APIs hide?

options.text: Capacity planning, batching/throughput tuning, warm-up, hardware utilization, model provenance verification, and security patching: the platform team you become
None; local models run themselves
Only electricity bills
Prompt writing

explanation: The API fee was buying operations. Self-hosting's TCO includes the engineering time that replaces it: count it before celebrating per-token savings.

prompt: An architecture decision record (ADR) for adopting/rejecting a technique should include…

options.text: …the evidence compared (baseline vs. candidate on your evals), costs, migration effort, fallback, and a review date, so future engineers know why, and when to reconsider
…only the final choice
…marketing materials from the vendor
…nothing; decisions speak for themselves

explanation: Decisions with recorded evidence survive team changes and hype cycles. 'Hold, revisit in Q2 when X matures' is a complete, successful outcome.

prompt: A team wants to fine-tune because 'the prompt is getting long.' The first question is…

options.text: …whether prompt caching already makes the long stable prefix nearly free: fine-tuning to save cached tokens usually buys complexity for pennies
…which GPU to buy
…how many epochs to run
…nothing; long prompts always justify tuning

explanation: Climb the ladder in order: the caching rung (Module 8) often dissolves the stated motivation before the fine-tuning rung is reached.

prompt: Choosing between a base model and an instruct/chat model for fine-tuning: the instruct model is usually right when…

options.text: …your task is assistant-shaped (instructions in, helpful output): you're adjusting behavior on top of post-training rather than rebuilding it from a raw text-continuer
…never; base models are always better
…you want the model to forget safety training
…your data is under 10 examples

explanation: Start from the checkpoint closest to your target behavior. Base models suit research and heavy custom post-training; product fine-tunes start from instruct.
